title: Standard owner Lord Lebedev cuts £5m off price of London mansion
summary:
Son of a Russian billionaire cuts cost of Stud House in Hampton Court estate from £25m to £19.85m

Evgeny Lebedev, the son of a Russian billionaire and owner of the Standard newspaper, has…

blocks.text: Evgeny Lebedev, the son of a Russian billionaire and owner of the Standard newspaper, has cut £5m off the asking price for his London mansion.

The eight-bedroom Grade II-listed house sits on the Hampton Court estate, a former hunting ground of King Henry VIII on the south-west edge of London. It was first listed in July for £25m, but that has been reduced to £19.85m.

Prices have dropped sharply in some of London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods such as Belgravia and Knightsbridge, amid a broader slowdown in the capital’s luxury property market. Many wealthy international buyers are thought to have been put off by the end of the non-dom regime as well as higher property taxes.

Even with the £5m reduction, which was first reported by the Telegraph, the purchase could trigger a stamp duty charge of as much as £3m. The buyer will also have to pay an extra £7,500 in “high-value council tax surcharge” from 2028 when the new mansion tax comes into effect.
Lebedev, who was appointed to the House of Lords by Boris Johnson in 2020, has been searching for a buyer for the property for at least five months.
The cross-bench peer, whose formal title is Baron Lebedev of Hampton and Siberia, is also facing losses at the Standard. His family bought the newspaper, formerly the Evening Standard, in 2009.
The 200-year-old paper reported a pre-tax loss of £8.3m in the 15-month period to 31 December 2025.

blocks.caption: Evgeny Lebedev at his Hampton Court mansion, known as the Stud House, in Bushy Park, London. Photograph: Tom Jamieson/The New York Times/Redux/eyevine

blocks.text: Lebedev is also one of the owners of the digital-only Independent title. Last year he pulled the plug on London Live, the capital’s dedicated TV channel, after a decade of mounting losses.

His Hampton Court mansion, Stud House, was built in the early 18th century as residence of the master of the horse, a royal officer who historically oversaw the monarch’s horses, stables and coach houses.

The property covers more than 1,480 sq metres (16,000 sq ft) and sits on 2.5 hectares (6.3 acres) of land, according to the estate agent Knight Frank. The main house includes a grand reception hall, two “treatment rooms”, a drawing room, a library and a conservatory.
There is also a coach house on the grounds, which includes a gym with a sauna and an ice bath, and a games room.
The property was bought by Alexander Lebedev, Evgeny’s father and a former KGB officer, in 2007.

Evgeny Lebedev told the Financial Times in 2024 that when he viewed Stud House with his father “he was probably more in love with it than I was but I can see now, having grown older, that it’s a special house.”
